title: Leigh air disaster
summary: A Blériot 155 aircraft operating a Paris to Croydon service encountered a fire in the port upper engine at 3:27 pm GMT while cruising. The fire spread to the wing and the aircraft changed direction toward Penshurst Airfield. The tail sank while the aircraft gained brief height, then rolled over and dived to the ground where it burned. This was the first recorded in-flight fire on an airliner.

title: 1934 Swissair Tuttlingen accident
summary: Swissair Condor II CH-170 cruising at 3,000 meters encountered a thunderstorm shortly after crossing the Swiss-German border. The right wing experienced structural failure from oscillation-induced stress fractures, exacerbated by violent turbulence. The wing separated from the fuselage and the aircraft fell into a forest near Tuttlingen, exploding on impact. All 12 occupants, including Europe's first air stewardess Nelly Diener, were killed.

title: 1934 KLM Douglas DC-2 crash
summary: KLM Douglas DC-2 Uiver crashed during a publicity flight from Cairo to Baghdad in a rainstorm and burst into flames near Rutbah Wells, killing all seven crew and passengers. The investigation revealed KLM had taken excessive risks, ignored multiple important safety aspects, and the aircraft had incomplete maintenance adjustments. The Dutch Minister issued airworthiness certificate with fewer demands than required. Poor weather conditions combined with inadequate aircraft preparation contributed to the accident.

title: 1938 Yosemite TWA crash
summary: A Douglas DC-2 encountered severe weather during descent from San Francisco to Winslow and diverted toward Fresno. The pilot experienced ice formation on wings and confusion about position relative to the Fresno Radio Range station. A sharp increase in wind velocity combined with the pilot's positional confusion resulted in flight over mountainous terrain in Yosemite National Park, ending in a crash.

events.text: Flight 8 was flying from San Francisco to Winslow, which was a hub connecting TWA's transcontinental route.

Captain Graves noticed ice forming on the wings and advised air traffic controllers, who ordered him to divert to Los Angeles due to the deteriorating weather conditions.
At 9:28 PM, he requested a weather update; this was his last transmission received by air traffic control and the aircraft subsequently crashed on a mountain in Yosemite National Park.

title: Kweilin Incident
summary: A Douglas DC-2 airliner named Kweilin operated by China National Aviation Corporation was shot down by eight Japanese pontoon-fitted aircraft on 24 August 1938 while flying from Hong Kong to Chengdu. The aircraft was unarmed and pilot Hugh Leslie Woods made a perfect water landing in a river when attacked. The Japanese continued strafing the aircraft for about an hour, riddling it with bullets until it sank. Fifteen of 18 aboard died including prominent Chinese bankers.

title: Crash of Halifax V9977
summary: On June 7, 1942, Handley Page Halifax V9977, being used as a flying testbed for the H2S radar by TRE, encountered an engine fire in its outboard starboard Rolls-Royce Merlin engine at 4:20 pm while flying over the Forest of Dean. The left wing broke off and the aircraft rolled over and crashed near Welsh Bicknor. All eleven crew members were killed, including inventor Alan Blumlein. Investigators determined improper engine maintenance and assembly procedures caused tappet valves to work loose, leading to engine failure.
probable_cause: Improper engine maintenance and assembly procedures caused the accident. Rolls-Royce had installed tappet valves with reduced clearance to prevent them working loose, but in field maintenance the lock nuts holding the valves in place were not properly reinstalled with correct clearance, allowing the tappet valves to work loose and causing the engine fire.

title: Lady Be Good
summary: B-24D Liberator Lady Be Good, a new aircraft with a first-time crew on their first combat mission, bombed Naples on April 4, 1943. On return, a sandstorm caused the crew to overshoot their air base at Soluch in Libya. The crew failed to realize they had overflown the base in the sandstorm and continued flying south into the Libyan Desert for many hours. When fuel was exhausted, eight of the nine crew members bailed out successfully. The survivors walked in the desert for eight days with only a single canteen of water to share, believing they were close to the Mediterranean coast. All nine crew members ultimately died.
probable_cause: The first-time crew failed to realize they had overflown their air base in a sandstorm. After continuing to fly south into the desert for many hours, the crew bailed out when the plane's fuel was exhausted. The survivors then died in the desert trying to walk to safety, unaware they were 400 miles inland.

Lady Be Good's crew were also new, having only arrived in Libya a week before on March 18, and they flew their first mission together on April 4.

A diary recovered from co-pilot Robert Toner indicated that none of the men were aware they had been flying over land when they bailed out, or that they were 400 miles inland. It has been speculated the dark empty desert floor may have resembled open sea.

title: Freckleton Air Disaster
summary: At approximately 10:36 on 23 August 1944, two newly refurbished B-24 aircraft departed Base Air Depot No. 2 on scheduled test flights. Test pilot First Lieutenant John Bloemendal was flying an aircraft designated Classy Chassis II. The pilots flew north at low altitude and encountered a violent incoming thunderstorm with reduced visibility. Both pilots were ordered to land at once at 10:41 a.m. First Lieutenant Bloemendal, flying at low altitude with reduced visibility, began struggling against violent turbulence and ordered his co-pilot to gain altitude. The aircraft crashed into the centre of the village of Freckleton, Lancashire, killing all three crewmen and 58 individuals on the ground, including 38 children. An official inquiry was unable to pinpoint an exact cause but noted the report was unable to discount structural failure in extreme weather conditions.

title: 1946 Australian National Airways DC-3 crash
summary: Australian National Airways Flight VH-AET departed Hobart on March 10, 1946, with 21 passengers and 3 pilots, one of whom was a supernumerary pilot on his first flights with the airline. title: BSAA Star Dust accident
summary: Star Dust, an Avro Lancastrian on charter from Buenos Aires to Santiago, crashed into Mount Tupungato at 15,000 feet after penetrating the poorly understood jet stream. The crew, believing they had cleared the mountain range at 24,000 feet and monitoring their calculated ground speed as exceeding their actual speed due to a headwind, descended into cloud-covered peaks they could not see. The aircraft hit the mountain at cruising speed with undercarriage retracted, indicating controlled flight into terrain. The wreckage was not found for 51 years, emerging from the Tupungato Glacier.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from controlled flight into terrain caused by navigational error. The crew mistakenly believed they had already cleared the Andes mountains and commenced descent when they were still a considerable distance to the east-northeast. This navigational error was likely caused by the crew's unfamiliarity with the jet stream, which produced an unexpected headwind that reduced their ground speed below their calculated assumptions, making them believe they were further west than they actually were.

factors.evidence: The aircraft crashed into Mount Tupungato at approximately 15,000 feet altitude, striking the mountain while in controlled flight with engines running near cruising speed and undercarriage retracted.

The crew mistakenly assumed their ground speed to be faster than it really was and deduced that they had already safely crossed the Andes, whereas they were still a considerable distance to the east-northeast and approaching the cloud-enshrouded Tupungato Glacier at high speed.
In the absence of visual sightings of the ground due to heavy clouds, the crew did not maintain awareness of their actual position relative to terrain.
Heavy clouds blocked visibility of the ground during the final portion of Star Dust's flight, preventing visual confirmation of position or terrain avoidance.
The jet stream phenomenon was not well understood in 1947, and the aircraft's navigation systems did not account for wind direction changes with altitude that the crew could not observe.

events.text: Aircraft cruising at 24,000 feet to cross Andes mountain range between Buenos Aires and Santiago.
Aircraft entered jet stream zone with headwind component, reducing actual ground speed significantly below crew's calculated assumptions.
Crew, mistakenly believing they had already cleared the mountain peaks, began descent toward Santiago.
Aircraft descended into cloud layers obscuring the cloud-covered Tupungato Glacier ahead, with no visual references available.

Aircraft impacted Mount Tupungato at high speed while in controlled flight, burying itself in snow and ice; the last Morse code transmission STENDEC was received by Santiago airport control tower four minutes before planned landing.

notes: Wreckage discovered in 1998 and 2000 in Tupungato Glacier at 15,000 feet elevation after 51+ years; previously missing.
The final Morse code transmission STENDEC has never been satisfactorily explained and remains a historical mystery.
Crew included experienced former RAF pilots; Captain Reginald Cook had DSO and DFC from WWII service.

title: United Air Lines 608

As the aircraft descended toward Bryce Canyon Airport, pieces of the aircraft including the right wing fell off. The crew was unable to maintain control in canyon gusts despite being only 10 feet above ground, and the aircraft crashed on National Park Service land. The fire and structural damage resulted from a design flaw in the cabin heater intake scoop placement relative to the fuel tank vent.
probable_cause: Design flaw: a cabin heater intake scoop was positioned too close to the number 3 alternate fuel tank air vent. When the fuel tank was overfilled during routine transfer, excess fuel was sucked into the cabin heater system and ignited. Contributing factors were inadequate crew training about the danger and failure to halt the fuel transfer before tank overflow.

title: 1948 Gatow air disaster
summary: A BEA Vickers Viking airliner on approach to RAF Gatow in West Berlin was struck by a Soviet Yakovlev Yak-3 fighter aircraft. The right engine caught fire during takeoff; smoke was observed by ATC and ground personnel. The crew attempted to lower the landing gear when warned, but fire spread progressively. The aircraft crashed into buildings and the Elizabeth Water Company property. Investigation determined that hold-down studs of the right engine's number 10 cylinder had failed, setting off the fire that brought down the aircraft.

Flying under visual reference only, the aircraft descended below prescribed minimums and struck Bucktooth Ridge at 2375 feet elevation. Fourteen survivors were in the aft passenger compartment.

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 324
summary: Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 324, a Douglas C-54E military charter aircraft, crashed into Hecate Strait in British Columbia while making an emergency landing at Sandspit Airport on January 19, 1952. Engine No. 1 failed near Sitka, and the crew declared an emergency and proceeded to Sandspit on three engines. During the landing approach, the aircraft touched down about one-third down the runway, then power was reapplied at midpoint to attempt a go-around. The aircraft became airborne but settled into Hecate Strait off the end of the runway. Seven survivors were rescued from the freezing waters, while the remaining 36 perished from drowning or exposure to cold temperatures.
probable_cause: Engine No. 1 suffered an oil loss necessitating engine shutdown. Following the engine failure, the crew elected to land at the nearest suitable airport rather than continue to destination on three engines, consistent with company procedures. The aborted landing and go-around attempt resulted in the aircraft settling into the water during climbout.

title: 1952 Air France SNCASE Languedoc crash
summary: The aircraft crashed shortly after takeoff from Nice Airport when the co-pilot's aileron controls jammed due to a chain slipping off its sprocket. The aircraft banked to the left, rolled onto its back and crashed about 1 km north of the airport, killing all 38 people on board. A design fault in the difficulty of setting and inspecting the chains in dual control columns contributed to the accident.

title: KLM 592
summary: The Douglas DC-6 departed Rome-Ciampino for Frankfurt Airport on 22 March 1952. At approximately 10:45 AM, the crew reported descending to 2,460 feet near the Offenbach beacon. Nothing more was heard from the flight, and the aircraft crashed into a forest approximately five minutes later. Of 47 occupants, 45 perished. The cause could not be determined, but investigation suggested the crew may have continued the approach below the minimum descent altitude to maintain visual contact with the ground.

title: Pan Am 526A
summary: Pan Am Flight 526A ditched in the Atlantic Ocean after both engines lost power shortly after takeoff from San Juan. Engine number 3 failed at 350 feet and engine number 4 failed at 550 feet. The investigation revealed inadequate maintenance: engine 3 had not been changed when metal shavings were found in the engine oil, leading to its failure immediately after takeoff. The crew performed a water landing, but survivors panicked and refused to board life rafts, resulting in 52 deaths.

title: Pan Am 202
summary: A Boeing 377 Stratocruiser registered N1039V, christened Clipper Good Hope, was operating an international scheduled passenger flight from Rio de Janeiro to Port of Spain, the third leg of a four-leg journey from Buenos Aires. The aircraft departed Rio at 2:43 a.m. on April 29, 1952 and was last heard from at 6:16 a.m. reporting abeam the city of Barreiras in eastern Brazil at 14,500 feet. It was expected to report abeam Carolina at 7:45 a.m. but the aircraft never reported again. Investigation of the wreckage found evidence indicating the No. 2 engine and propeller had failed in flight, causing the aircraft to break apart. It crashed in the dense Amazon jungle approximately 281 nautical miles southwest of Carolina. All 50 people aboard were killed.
probable_cause: The exact cause of the crash was not established. title: 1952 Farnborough Airshow DH.110 crash
summary: During an aerobatic display at the Farnborough Airshow, a prototype de Havilland DH.110 jet disintegrated in flight. Following a supersonic dive and flypast from 40,000 feet and during a left bank at about 450 knots toward the crowd, the pilot pulled up into a climb. In less than a second, the outer sections of the wing, both engines and the cockpit separated from the airframe. Debris fell onto spectators, killing 29 and injuring 60. The investigation showed the wing had only 64% of its intended strength.
probable_cause: Structural failure due to a design flaw in the wing's leading edge, with the outer section of the wing failing because it had only 64% of its intended strength.

title: BOAC 783
summary: BOAC Flight 783, a de Havilland Comet jetliner registered G-ALYV, broke up in mid-air and crashed six minutes after taking off from Calcuttas Dum Dum Airport on May 2, 1953. The aircraft was climbing to 7,500 feet when radio contact was lost. Witnesses near the village of Jagalgori, approximately 25 miles northwest of Calcutta, observed the aircraft coming down in flames amid severe rain and thunderstorms. The wreckage was strewn along a five-mile track with main parts still on fire. All 43 occupants were killed.

title: Tachikawa air disaster
summary: A United States Air Force Douglas C-124A Globemaster II crashed on June 18, 1953, three minutes after takeoff from Tachikawa Air Base, Japan. The aircraft's No. 1 outer left engine burst into flames one minute into the flight. The commander shut down the engine and declared return to base, requesting ground-controlled approach. However, during return procedures the left wing stalled, causing the aircraft to roll left into an unrecoverable dive. The aircraft crashed into a watermelon patch 3.5 miles from the airbase, killing all 129 people aboard. The investigation determined the crash was caused by improper flap usage and airspeed loss following the port engine failure.

title: 1953 Sabena Convair Crash
summary: A Sabena Convair CV-240 crashed approximately three kilometers north of Frankfurt International Airport shortly after takeoff on October 14, 1953. The crew noticed both engines losing power shortly after liftoff and attempted to raise the flaps and maintain control, but the aircraft became uncontrollable and stalled, crashing in a wooded area near Kelsterbach. All 44 occupants perished in the wreckage fire.
probable_cause: Heavy deposit of lead on spark plugs in both engines. As the plugs warmed during takeoff, metal deposits formed a circuit that short-circuited the plugs, causing fatal engine failure and subsequent stalling and crash. It is unknown whether pilot actions contributed to the outcome or if the fatal outcome was unavoidable.

title: BOAC 781
summary: BOAC Flight 781, a De Havilland Comet jet, crashed on January 10, 1954, following an explosive decompression at altitude. The aircraft had departed Rome on the final leg to London when, at approximately 10:50, the cabin explosively depressurized and the fuselage broke apart, with debris falling into the sea near Elba, Italy. Investigation revealed the failure initiated in the roof of the cabin, propagating through the fuselage, with the tail section failing and outer wing structure collapsing. This was the second of three fatal Comet structural failures within twelve months, indicating systematic design or manufacturing vulnerabilities.

The crew then made an inexplicable right turn away from the favorable Green 1 airway into the border mountains while reporting they were on Green 1. Flying in severe icing conditions with one engine shut down, the aircraft crashed into Mount Slesse at excessive speed.
probable_cause: Combination of airframe icing and engine shutdown, combined with navigation error placing the aircraft in terrain causing controlled flight into terrain.

factors.evidence: combination of several factors with the main ones being icing of the wings and fuselage

the aircraft turned away from Green 1 rather than toward it and wound up heading west-southwest 12 miles south of Green 1
aircraft flew straight into the third peak of Mount Slesse well in excess of cruising speed
plane crashed into Mount Slesse in remote terrain

events.text: Flight 810-9 left Vancouver International Airport at 6:10 p.m. on December 9, 1956.
The pilots climbed to 19,200 feet and experienced a fire warning indication in engine number two.
Engine number two was shut down as a precaution because false fire warnings in North Star aircraft had been noted on numerous previous occasions.
The pilot inexplicably made a right turn and wound up heading west-southwest 12 miles south of Green 1 straight into the border mountains.
At 7:10, the plane radioed that they were passing Hope and was given clearance to descend to 8000 feet.
The aircraft flew in severe icing conditions with one engine shut down over the mountains.
The plane crashed into the third peak of Mount Slesse well in excess of cruising speed.

title: Northeast Airlines 823
summary: Northeast Airlines Flight 823, a Douglas DC-6, crashed shortly after takeoff from LaGuardia in poor visibility. The captain entered cloud cover and lost spatial awareness on instruments, executing an incorrect left turn instead of the assigned northeast heading. The aircraft descended below terrain clearance and crashed into trees on Rikers Island, killing 20 passengers.
probable_cause: The failure of the captain to properly observe and interpret his flight instruments, and to maintain control of his aircraft.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was flying on instruments without outside visibility as it headed over Flushing Bay.
The captain lost spatial awareness when he entered the clouds seconds after takeoff, therefore didn't detect or correct the airplane's deviation from its desired course.
The airplane began a gradual turn to the left, and when it had reached a heading of 285° (nearly due west), it overflew Rikers Island.
Its altitude was insufficient to clear the trees on the island, and the aircraft crashed.

events.text: Delays due to snowfall pushed departure back; the airplane was cleared to take off via runway 04 at 6:01 PM.
Upon establishing a positive rate of climb, the landing gear and wing flaps were retracted.
Aircraft entered cloud cover flying on instruments without outside visibility.
The aircraft came to rest within 1,500 ft of the point of first impact after crashing into trees on Rikers Island.

title: Aviaco 111
summary: The aircraft entered an unrecoverable right-hand spin during approach after the captain spotted a green landing signal from the control tower. Distracted by the need to visually confirm landing clearance through tower signals rather than radio communication, the captain lost situational awareness and the aircraft crashed near the airport before reaching the runway.
probable_cause: Pilot error and loss of situational awareness resulting from distraction caused by reliance on visual signals from the control tower due to radio communication failure.

title: LOT Polish Airlines 232
summary: LOT Polish Airlines Flight 232, an Ilyushin Il-14P, crashed near Vnukovo Airport while descending in poor weather after being instructed to descend to 300 meters. The investigation determined the pilot failed to comply with the prescribed instrument approach procedure, descending to an extremely low altitude. The aircraft struck the ground at high speed in very low ceiling conditions with heavy turbulence and rain, killing 9 people including the pilot, co-pilot, and two crew members.
probable_cause: The aircraft hit the ground while flying at an excessively low altitude following the crew's application of an approach procedure other than that prescribed by Vnukovo Aerodrome. Bad weather conditions with low ceiling and heavy rain that were not forecast in the messages influenced the disastrous outcome.

title: KLM 844
summary: After takeoff at night from Biak-Mokmer Airport, the captain requested and received permission to perform a low pass down the runway with runway lights kept on. During a 180-degree turn at low altitude, the aircraft lost altitude and struck the sea 1.2 km from departure, sinking in 250-meter-deep water. The pilot may have misjudged altitude relative to the sea in darkness.
probable_cause: No direct evidence of pilot error or technical failure. The aircraft may have struck the sea due to pilot misjudgment of altitude relative to the sea in darkness while performing a low pass maneuver on a scheduled passenger flight.

summary: Maritime Central Airways Flight 315, a Douglas DC-4 on charter from London to Toronto with stops in Reykjavík and Goose Bay, crashed in bad weather near Issoudun, Quebec. While flying at approximately 6,000 feet near Quebec City, the aircraft flew into a cumulonimbus cloud, encountered severe turbulence, and lost control in a near-vertical dive.

title: Pan Am 7
summary: Pan Am Flight 7, a Boeing 377 Stratocruiser with 44 aboard, disappeared en route from San Francisco to Honolulu on November 8, 1957. The aircraft made a routine position report at 5:04 p.m. while 1028 nautical miles east of Hawaii but was never heard from again approximately nine hours later when fuel would have been exhausted. No emergency signals were received. The CAB concluded it did not have enough evidence to determine the cause of the accident.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board could not determine the cause of the accident. The aircraft disappeared without any emergency signal after approximately nine hours of flight when fuel reserves would have been exhausted.

factors.evidence: Aircraft had enough fuel for approximately thirteen hours of flight; crash occurred about nine hours after departure when aircraft would have exhausted fuel reserves.
Sabotage and in-flight fire were among theories explored but no definitive evidence found to support these causes.
Poor maintenance was speculated as possible cause, though CAB found aircraft, engines, and propellers had been maintained as prescribed.
Aircraft disappeared with bodies and wreckage eventually recovered, indicating structural failure or loss of control leading to impact with water.

events.text: Flight 7 departed San Francisco International Airport at 11:30 a.m. carrying 36 passengers and 8 crew members, maximum takeoff weight 147000 lb.
Captain made routine position report at 5:04 p.m. while aircraft was 1028 nautical miles east of Hawaii, cruising at 10000 ft altitude with headwinds of approximately 14 mph.
Expected position report around 6:00 p.m. was never received; aircraft disappeared from radar contact without any emergency signal.
After no communication for more than 90 minutes, Pan Am notified Coast Guard; extensive search found 19 bodies and aircraft pieces about 900 nautical miles northeast of Honolulu.

title: Aerolíneas Argentinas 670
summary: Aerolíneas Argentinas Flight 670, a Douglas DC-4, took off from Buenos Aires on 8 December 1957 bound for San Carlos de Bariloche with 61 occupants. The captain chose to fly at 328 to 492 feet instead of the cleared altitude of 3,937 to 7,874 feet in an attempt to avoid an intense cold front. The aircraft then climbed sharply to 8,202 feet and entered the worsening storm at its most active part. At this height, the left wing failed followed quickly by the tail section, and the aircraft dove uncontrollably into the ground. Investigation determined the aircraft disintegrated from severe turbulence stress after the pilot's reckless decision to fly into the storm.
probable_cause: Aircraft disintegrated from severe turbulence stress after pilot flew recklessly into active part of intense storm at high altitude

title: Munich air disaster
summary: British European Airways Flight 609, an Airspeed Ambassador en route from Belgrade to Manchester, stopped at Munich to refuel. After two aborted takeoff attempts due to engine boost surging, the crew attempted a third takeoff in snow and slush. The aircraft failed to become airborne, struck a fence at runway end, and the left wing was torn off when it struck a house beyond the runway. Altogether 23 died and 21 survived.

title: Winter Hill air disaster
summary: A Bristol 170 Freighter chartered by Manx Airlines carrying motor trade personnel from the Isle of Man to Manchester was cleared to maintain 1500 feet altitude due to traffic and poor weather. While the captain was briefly absent from the cockpit, the first officer erroneously tuned the radio compass to Oldham Beacon instead of the correct Wigan Beacon. Visibility was extremely poor and Manchester Control ordered an immediate right turn but the aircraft crashed near the summit of Winter Hill in heavy snow. Thirty-five of the 42 aboard were killed.
probable_cause: First officer's error tuning the radio compass to the wrong beacon; captain's failure to confirm the correct tuning. Inquiry also ascribed blame to air traffic controllers and the aircraft's cockpit design with difficult-to-see navigation displays.

Manchester Control at 9:44 AM ordered an immediate right turn when the mistake was first noticed.

title: United Airlines 736

location.name: Southwest of Las Vegas, Clark County, Nevada

summary: United Air Lines Flight 736, a Douglas DC-7 with 47 passengers and crew aboard, was flying at 21,000 feet over Clark County, Nevada, on April 21, 1958, when it collided in midair with a United States Air Force F-100F Super Sabre fighter jet crewed by two pilots. Both aircraft fell out of control and crashed into unpopulated desert terrain southwest of Las Vegas, leaving no survivors. The collision occurred in clear weather at high altitude with high closure speeds. The investigation determined that structural supports on both aircraft's canopies limited pilot visibility and contributed to the inability to see the other aircraft until too late.
probable_cause: The high rate of near head-on closure and cockpit visibility limitations. A metal frame support on the F-100's canopy interfered with the Air Force instructor pilot's ability to see the oncoming DC-7, while a supporting pillar on the DC-7's windshield could have prevented the United Airlines captain from sighting the fighter until too late.

factors.evidence: The DC-7 airliner collided with the F-100F Super Sabre fighter jet at 21,000 feet.
ATC authorities at CAA and Nellis Air Force Base failed to reduce known collision risks and failed to coordinate traffic separation for training exercises.
A metal frame support on the F-100's canopy interfered with the Air Force instructor pilot's ability to see the oncoming DC-7.
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year.

The aircraft crashed into a hangar 600 meters past the runway, killing all 61 aboard.

title: Capital Airlines 300
summary: On 20 May 1958, a Vickers Viscount operated by Capital Airlines Flight 300 collided mid-air with a US Air Force Lockheed T-33 jet trainer in the airspace near Brunswick, Maryland. The Viscount had departed Pittsburgh for Baltimore at 10:50 local time and was descending through 8000 to 9000 feet when the T-33, traveling at significantly higher speed (290 knots versus 235 knots), banked right and impacted the left side of the Viscount forward of the wing. The Viscount pitched up, entered a steep spin, and crashed. All 11 people on the Viscount were killed; the T-33 pilot ejected and survived but was burned.

The crew lost situational awareness without visual references and did not correct the navigation error. The aircraft crashed into the mountain killing all 45 occupants.

title: KLM 607-E
summary: KLM Flight 607-E, a Lockheed Super Constellation named Hugo de Groot on the second leg of a transatlantic trip from Amsterdam to New York, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean after departing Shannon Airport, Ireland, on 14 August 1958. Radio contact was lost about 35 minutes after takeoff, and a rescue operation later found light debris and recovered the remains of 34 of the 99 people aboard roughly 180 km northwest of Shannon. Irish and Dutch investigators could not pinpoint a definitive cause but believed the most likely explanation was an over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing an oil feed line regulator valve, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.
probable_cause: Investigators could not determine a definitive cause but considered the most likely explanation to be a malfunctioning over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing oil feed line regulator valves, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.

title: Aeroflot 4
summary: The Tu-104A departed Khabarovsk and climbed to avoid towering cumulus clouds, reaching 12,000 m despite this being unsafe at the aircraft's takeoff weight of 66 tons. The aircraft encountered intense cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts that caused the aircraft to stall. Both engines flamed out during the stall, and the artificial horizons failed, rendering recovery nearly impossible.
probable_cause: The aircraft was flown to an unsafe altitude given its weight and encountered severe updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds, resulting in an aerodynamic stall. Insufficient analysis of weather conditions and lack of stall recovery procedures contributed to the accident.

factors.evidence: The aircraft climbed to 12000 m while weighted at 66 tons; altitudes of 12000 m could only be safely achieved in calm weather, and the weight limited maximum safe altitude to 11700 m at standard engine power.
Cumulonimbus clouds reaching altitudes of over 12000 m with strong updrafts between 11000 and the reported presence of strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds.
There were no defined procedures in place in the event of a stall, indicating lack of crew training for this situation.
The Tu-104 was prone to losing longitudinal stability in certain atmospheric conditions, could be followed by engine failure and artificial horizon failure.
The aircraft stalled, during which the engines flamed out and the landing gear was extended.
The aircraft crashed into a dense forest 215 km northwest of Khabarovsk airport, impacting the ground at an angle of 60°.

summary: A Vickers Viking operated by Independent Air Travel took off from London Heathrow but reported engine problems within minutes and requested return to Blackbushe Airport. Unable to maintain descent altitude, the aircraft continued descending and issued a Mayday call before crashing into a row of houses in Southall. The public inquiry found serious operational flaws: maintenance performed by unqualified personnel, aircraft overloaded, pilot fatigued from 31.5 hours on duty, and inadequate check flights.

title: 1958 Aeroflot Tu-104 crash in Chuvash
summary: Aeroflot Flight CCCP-42362, a Tupolev Tu-104A, was diverted from Moscow-Vnukovo due to heavy fog and proceeded to higher altitudes when flying into strong turbulence. The aircraft reached 12,000 meters altitude before entering a sharp, near-vertical dive and spin. The crew was unable to overcome the control forces and the aircraft crashed near Kanash. The investigation determined the crash was caused by loss of control from flying into strong turbulence causing the aircraft to exceed critical angles of attack.

While in descent approach to Krasnoyarsk, the crew transmitted an incoherent emergency call with unusual background noise before the aircraft crashed 28 kilometers east of Krasnoyarsk Airport, impacting the ground upside-down at a 40-degree angle. The official investigation concluded the cause was stall and loss of spatial disorientation in cloud. An alternative theory suggests an anti-aircraft missile that went astray during an air defense exercise struck the aircraft.

title: Alitalia 771
summary: Alitalia Flight 771, a multi-leg service from Sydney to Rome, crashed into a hill about 84 km north-east of Bombay on approach on 7-8 July 1962, killing all 94 aboard. Investigators found navigational errors led the captain, on his first familiarization trip over the Bangkok-Bombay leg, to believe he was closer to his destination than he actually was, causing a premature descent for a straight-in instrument approach at night; the aircraft continued down to 3,600 ft, below both the 9,000 ft minimum safety altitude and the 4,000 ft minimum initial approach altitude, before striking terrain.

title: Aeroflot 415
summary: Aeroflot Flight 415, an Antonov An-10, departed Simferopol at 14:37 on 28 July 1962 bound for Sochi. While descending through mountainous terrain, the aircraft crashed into a 700-meter mountain at an altitude of 500 meters. Investigation attributed the accident to multiple errors: ATC failed to inform the crew about clouds at approximately 600 meters on nearby mountains, gave an insufficient turn instruction of only 20 degrees when 60 degrees minimum was needed to avoid terrain, and the crew lacked adequate preparation for the approach to Sochi.

title: Flying Tiger Line 923
summary: A Lockheed Constellation L-1049H ditched in the North Atlantic on September 23, 1962 while attempting to divert to Shannon, Ireland. Engine 3 fire warning sounded at 20:19 GMT and the engine was shut down. Six to seven minutes later, the flight engineer pulled the firewall lever for engine 1 instead of engine 3, shutting down the functioning engine and leaving the aircraft with only two engines. Engine 2 caught fire at 21:25 GMT and power was reduced. Engine 2 failed at around 21:57 GMT, causing loss of hydraulic pressure. The aircraft ditched into waves 200 feet apart, the left wing tore off, and only one of five rafts was usable. 48 of 76 survived six hours on the overcrowded raft.

title: United Airlines 297
summary: A Vickers Viscount 745D was cleared to descend from 10,000 to 6,000 feet during a scheduled flight from Newark to Atlanta. At 12:19 p.m. controllers advised the crew of numerous reports of large numbers of ducks and geese in the area. At 6,000 feet the aircraft struck two whistling swans with its stabilizers. One swan caused superficial damage to the right stabilizer while the other crashed completely through the left stabilizer and separated it from the aircraft. The loss of the left stabilizer caused immediate loss of control; the aircraft's altitude dropped to ground level in less than a minute. It crashed 10 miles southwest of Baltimore, killing all 17 aboard.

summary: Varig Flight 810 crashed into the Laz Cruz Peak while maneuvering for an approach to Lima on 27 November 1962, killing all 97 aboard. An overestimate of seven minutes in the flight-planned time between Pisco and Lima left the Boeing 707 too high for a straight-in approach to runway 33, so ATC had the crew fly a 360-degree orbit and turns to intercept the ILS back course; during this extended maneuvering the aircraft deviated eight miles east of the published approach track and struck the peak at a heading of 333 degrees. Investigators suggested the pilot may have mistuned the Limatambo NDB for the Lima NDB.

title: New Zealand National Airways Corporation 441
summary: A Douglas DC-3 Skyliner operating Flight 441 from Auckland to Tauranga flew into a vertical rock face in the Kaimai Ranges at 2,460 feet altitude on 3 July 1963 at approximately 9:09 am NZST. The Civil Aviation Authority investigation found that a downdraft carried the aircraft below the level of the range crests into an area of extreme turbulence from which the crew could not recover altitude. The investigation noted that under very poor weather conditions and probably unaware of their true position, the crew initiated a premature descent to the officially designated minimum safe altitude for the area. Another aircraft was caught in strong downdrafts the same day but managed to recover. Twenty-two of the 23 people aboard were killed instantly; one person survived the impact but died shortly afterward. Three extra passengers who were supposed to be on the flight changed their plans at the last minute.

title: Swissair 306
summary: Flight 306 took off from Zurich in dense fog and reached 2700 meters altitude four minutes after takeoff. A white trail of smoke was observed from the left side of the aircraft, followed by a long flame from the left wing. The aircraft entered a gentle left turn and began descending more steeply into a final dive. A Mayday was issued and the aircraft crashed near Dürrenäsch. The accident resulted from overheated aircraft brakes during taxiing through fog at full engine power, causing magnesium wheels to burst.
probable_cause: Aircraft brakes overheated from application of full engine power during taxiing to disperse fog. Magnesium wheels burst, with one bursting on the runway before departure. Spilled hydraulic fluid ignited when contacting overheated landing gear rims, causing fire in the gear bay that spread to the wing. The resulting electrical problems and structural damage led to loss of control.

title: 1966 Palomares B-52 crash
summary: A B-52G bomber collided with a KC-135 tanker during mid-air refueling at 31,000 feet over the Mediterranean Sea near Palomares, Spain. title: 1969 Aswan Ilyushin Il-18 crash
summary: An Ilyushin Il-18 operated by United Arab Airlines, carrying Hajj pilgrims from Jeddah to Aswan, made two unsuccessful landing attempts in darkness with visibility reduced to 2-3 kilometers by a sandstorm on 20 March 1969. On a third approach the aircraft banked right and hit the left side of the runway, tearing off the starboard wing; the resulting fuel spillage caused the wreckage to burst into flames, killing 100 of the 105 aboard. Investigators found the pilot had descended below the minimum safe altitude without the runway lights clearly in sight, and cited fatigue from continuous working hours without suitable rest as a contributory factor.

The Il-14 disobeyed ATC instructions and climbed to 3000 m to avoid turbulence, where the An-12 formation was flying. All 120 occupants of both aircraft perished.

title: Aeroflot 826
summary: Aeroflot Flight N-826, an Antonov An-24B, crashed on 3 August 1969 during climb to 4200 meters near Preobrazhenka, Ukraine. The propeller blade punctured the fuselage, severing all control cables for the stabilizer, ailerons, and rudder, rendering the aircraft uncontrollable. The aircraft spiraled down and struck the ground at a steep angle at 500-550 km/h.

title: Allegheny Airlines 853
summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9, collided mid-air with a privately owned Piper PA-28 near Fairland, Indiana, on September 9, 1969. The DC-9 was on an instrument flight plan descending for approach to Indianapolis at 3,550 feet when it converged with the VFR Piper aircraft at a relative speed of 350 mph. The left wing of the PA-28 sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly. Both aircraft lost control and crashed, killing all 83 occupants on both aircraft. The collision resulted from deficiencies in air traffic control radar capabilities, the see-and-avoid concept under mixed IFR/VFR conditions, and the absence of regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic in terminal areas.
probable_cause: The deficiencies in the collision avoidance capability of the Air Traffic Control system in a terminal area with mixed IFR and VFR traffic. The deficiencies included inadequacy of the see-and-avoid concept, technical limitations of radar in detecting all aircraft, and absence of Federal Aviation Regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic.

The FAA system lacked adequate regulations for separating mixed IFR and VFR traffic in terminal areas.
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year.

events.text: Flight 1903 departed Manchester Airport at 16:08 BST and encountered air traffic control delays in the Paris area, resulting in a change of route.
Radio contact was established with Barcelona Area Control Centre at 17:53 local time, and the crew was cleared to descend from Flight Level 220 to FL090.
Six minutes later the flight was handed to Barcelona approach control, which cleared the crew to overfly the Sabadell NDB and descend further to FL060.
While carrying out the turn, the crew reported in error that they had passed the Sabadell NDB, though they were still 28 nautical miles north of it, over the Serralada del Montseny.
Barcelona ATC mistook the radar echo of another aircraft overflying Sabadell for the Dan-Air Comet and cleared the crew to continue descending to 2800 ft.
At about 19:05 CEST the Comet struck a group of beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3800 ft and was destroyed in the explosion.

title: Flight 2605 by Western Airlines

title: Advance Airlines 4210
summary: Advance Airlines Flight 4210 crashed into a seawall at Sydney Airport 106 seconds after takeoff when the left engine failed at 150 feet. title: Saudia 163

title: 1981 Pushkin Tu-104 crash
summary: Tupolev Tu-104A aircraft crashed during takeoff from Pushkin Airport near Leningrad on 7 February 1981, killing all 50 on board. title: Space Shuttle Challenger disaster
summary: Space Shuttle Challenger disintegrated 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986, when record-low ambient temperatures stiffened the O-ring seals in the right Solid Rocket Booster's aft joint. Hot pressurized gas leaked through the compromised joint, burning through the attachment strut to the external tank. The structural failure led to rotation of the SRB and aerodynamic forces that tore the orbiter apart at Mach 1.92 approximately 46,000 feet above the Atlantic Ocean, killing all seven crew members instantly.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by the failure of the O-ring seals in the aft joint of the right Solid Rocket Booster. Record-low temperatures on launch morning stiffened the O-ring material, reducing its ability to seal the joint. The compromised seals allowed hot pressurized gas to escape, which burned through the aft attachment strut and the external tank. This structural failure caused the SRB to rotate, creating aerodynamic forces that destroyed the orbiter at Mach 1.92.

title: Ramstein air show disaster

title: 1990 Guangzhou Baiyun airport collisions
summary: On 2 October 1990, a hijacked Boeing 737-200 operating Xiamen Airlines Flight 8301 collided with two other aircraft at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport while attempting to land. The hijacked aircraft struck parked China Southwest Airlines Flight 4305, a Boeing 707, first, then collided with CAAC Flight 3523, a Boeing 757 waiting to take off, flipping onto its back. A total of 128 people were killed, including seven of nine crew members and 75 of 93 passengers on Flight 8301 and 46 of 110 passengers on Flight 3523, making the incident the deadliest aircraft hijacking prior to the September 11 attacks.

title: Alitalia 404
summary: Alitalia Flight 404, a DC-9, was on approach to Zurich Airport when the captain's instrument landing system display malfunctioned due to a faulty NAV receiver, incorrectly indicating the aircraft was 1,000 feet higher than its actual altitude. The first officer's ILS display was working correctly and showed the dangerously low approach. Without thoroughly examining which value was correct, the captain decided to ignore the first officer and aborted the first officer's go-around attempt. The aircraft subsequently struck Stadlerberg Mountain at 1,660 feet, killing all 46 occupants. The faulty receiver also prevented the autopilot and ground proximity warning system from receiving proper signals.
probable_cause: A short circuit in the captain's NAV receiver caused it to display incorrect altitude information while preventing the autopilot and GPWS from functioning. title: Bangkok Airways 125
summary: The Dash 8 was on approach to Samui Airport in bad weather when the crew decided to go around after losing sight of the runway. title: LAN Chile 1069

title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 2311
summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia with 23 aboard, crashed north of Brunswick, Georgia on April 5, 1991 during approach to landing. The NTSB investigation determined that the left propeller control unit malfunctioned, allowing the left propeller to overspeed with its blades oriented nearly perpendicular to the direction of flight. This created severe asymmetric thrust with insufficient thrust on the left side, causing a left roll that exceeded pilot recovery capability. The crew did not perceive the problem until the propeller blade angle reached 22-26 degrees, at which point the aircraft became very difficult to control.

title: Aeroflot 8556
summary: Aeroflot Flight 8556 crashed 13 meters short of the runway on approach to Pulkovo Airport. title: Lauda Air 004
summary: Lauda Air Flight 004, a Boeing 767-300ER flying from Hong Kong via Bangkok to Vienna, crashed into mountainous jungle terrain in Thailand on 26 May 1991 after the thrust reverser on the No. 1 engine deployed uncommanded during the climb. The pilots had received an EICAS advisory about a possible reverser fault nine minutes earlier but took no remedial action, believing it a false indication. The reverser deployment disrupted airflow over the wing, causing a 25% loss of lift and an aerodynamic stall; the aircraft entered a diving left turn and in-flight breakup, killing all 223 people on board.

title: Airbus Industrie 129

summary: TWA Flight 800, a Boeing 747 flying from New York to Rome via Paris, exploded in flight and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off East Moriches, New York, twelve minutes after takeoff on 17 July 1996, killing all 230 aboard. The four-year NTSB investigation concluded that flammable vapors in the center fuel tank ignited, likely from a short circuit, after finding arcing in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the tank; the captain had remarked on 'crazy' FQIS readings shortly before the explosion.
probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause was an explosion of flammable fuel/air vapors in the center wing fuel tank, most likely ignited by a short circuit, with evidence of arcing found in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the tank.

factors.evidence: Problems with the aircraft's wiring were found, including evidence of arcing in the fuel quantity indication system (FQIS) wiring that enters the tank.
The report's conclusion was that the probable cause of the accident was the explosion of flammable fuel vapors in the center fuel tank.
Several wide-ranging recommendations were made, which were incorporated into newer US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) standards.
The Boeing 747-100 performing this flight exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York, twelve minutes after takeoff.

events.text: About two minutes and thirty seconds before the explosion, the captain remarked about 'crazy' readings from the fuel quantity indication system.
At approximately 8:31 p.m. EDT, twelve minutes after takeoff, the Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York.
NTSB investigators found evidence of arcing in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the center fuel tank, a likely ignition source for the flammable vapors.
All 230 people on board were killed when the aircraft broke apart and crashed into the ocean, the deadliest air disaster investigation in U.S. history up to that time.
The four-year NTSB investigation approved its Aircraft Accident Report on August 23, 2000, and its recommendations were incorporated into new FAA fuel-tank safety standards.

title: Vnukovo Airlines 2801
summary: On approach to Svalbard Airport, the crew used outdated Jeppesen charts and set both HSIs to magnetic runway heading 283 degrees without using the localizer course. During the inbound turn, lateral deviation from the centerline grew due to inadequate wind drift correction. The aircraft reached Advent at 1,524 meters and turned late, resulting in a left (northeast) deviation from the correct track. Navigation at 1,524 m minimum altitude led to aircraft striking ground at Operafjellet during final approach, 3.7 km from the centerline.
probable_cause: A series of small navigational errors caused the aircraft to be 3.7 km from the approach centerline at the time of impact. The crew did not attempt to intercept the correct magnetic course and were probably not aware of VHF direction finding available at the airport.

title: Aeroperú 603
summary: Aeroperú Flight 603 experienced total loss of airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed indications due to adhesive tape left covering the static ports after maintenance. Flying at night over water without visual references, the crew received contradictory warnings and struggled to control the aircraft. Multiple stalls occurred during descent from an unknown altitude, and the aircraft eventually crashed into the Pacific Ocean.
probable_cause: Maintenance worker left adhesive tape covering the static ports after aircraft cleaning. This blocked the ports critical to all basic flight instruments, providing false and contradictory data to the flight crew and flight computers, preventing accurate control during the approach.

The investigation determined engine failure was the cause, with the aircraft in poor condition with documented corrosion and cracks.

title: TAM Transportes Aéreos Regionais 402
summary: TAM Flight 402 encountered an uncommanded thrust reverser deployment on the right engine while climbing away from runway 17R at Congonhas. The safety cable preventing reverser actuation parted at a maintenance connection when the copilot held the throttle fully open. With the right engine producing reverse thrust and the left engine at takeoff power, the aircraft rolled violently to the right and descended into buildings and houses only 25 seconds after takeoff.

Flight 086's TCAS warned of traffic and the crew attempted evasive action. Following the TCAS alert, Captain Sama took control, but ATC directed a heading that led to loss of control and the aircraft crashed inverted in Lagos Lagoon at high speed.

title: Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
summary: Saudia Flight 763, a Boeing 747 climbing out of Delhi, collided almost head-on over Charkhi Dadri on 12 November 1996 with Kazakhstan Airlines Flight 1907, an Ilyushin Il-76 descending toward Delhi, killing all 349 aboard both aircraft. The Lahoti Commission found the Kazakh crew, relying on a radio operator due to poor English skills, failed to level off at their assigned altitude and kept descending toward the Saudia jet, compounded by crew resource management failures; Delhi's radar had no altitude readout.
probable_cause: The Kazakh Il-76 crew's failure to maintain its cleared altitude, worsened by poor English comprehension of ATC instructions and crew resource management failures, caused the collision with the climbing Saudia 747.

The Kazakh crew reported reaching 15,000 feet, but the aircraft was actually higher, at 16,348 ft, and still descending.
Delhi airport lacked a secondary surveillance radar; the primary radar gave distance and bearing but not altitude.
The Il-76's left wing sliced through the 747's engines while the 747's stabilizer sliced off the Il-76's tail.

Both aircraft collided at the runway intersection and caught fire. All 14 occupants died from smoke inhalation.

title: Comair 3272
summary: Flight 3272 on approach to Detroit descended to 4,000 feet and was instructed to turn left to intercept the localizer. During the turn, the captain noted the low speed indicator and requested more power from the first officer. The aircraft abruptly stalled with a thin rough accretion of ice on the lifting surfaces. The aircraft rolled violently 145 degrees left, right, and left again as the crew lost control. The stall was attributed to inadequate icing procedures and failure to activate de-icing boots.
probable_cause: Aerodynamic stall and loss of control caused by aircraft encountering a thin rough accretion of ice on the wings while operating at a low airspeed in icing conditions. Contributing factors included inadequate FAA standards for icing operations, inadequate Comair procedures for icing conditions, crew failure to activate de-icing boots contrary to manufacturer recommendations, and operation near the lower end of the flight envelope while flaps were retracted.

title: 1997 Israeli helicopter disaster
summary: Two Israeli Air Force Sikorsky S-65C-3 transport helicopters departed Rosh Pina Airport for a mission to southern Lebanon security zone. After collecting troops, both helicopters were cleared to take off at 6:48 PM and hovered awaiting border clearance, which was granted at 6:56 PM. The Israeli investigation concluded the rotor of helicopter 357 struck the tail of helicopter 903. Helicopter 357 crashed immediately while the crew of 903 attempted recovery but failed and it crashed as well. All 73 military personnel aboard (two helicopters with crews totaling 8 and 65 passengers) were killed.

title: China Southern Airlines 3456
summary: China Southern Airlines Flight 3456 crashed at Shenzhen Bao'an on May 8, 1997 during a second attempt to land in a severe thunderstorm. The aircraft bounced hard on the first landing attempt and damaged its nose gear, hydraulic systems, and flaps. Debris from the damaged aircraft scattered across the runway. After a go-around with multiple system failures, the crew attempted a second landing on the damaged aircraft with debris contaminating the runway. During the second landing the aircraft skidded off the runway, broke into three pieces and caught fire.

title: Korean Air 801

summary: Korean Air Flight 801, a Boeing 747-300 flying from Seoul to Guam, crashed into Bijia Peak on approach to Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport on August 6, 1997, after Captain Park continued a non-precision approach in heavy rain despite the glideslope being out of service. First officer Song and flight engineer Nam noticed the steep descent and said the airport was not in sight, but the captain proceeded until the aircraft struck terrain below the minimum safe altitude, killing 229 of the 254 aboard.
probable_cause: The NTSB cited poor communication between the flight crew as the probable cause, along with the captain's poor decision-making on the non-precision approach.

Despite protests from Nam that the detected signal was not the glide-slope indicator, Park continued the approach.
The aircraft descended below the minimum safe altitude of 1440 ft during its landing approach.

title: Helikopter Service 451
summary: A Eurocopter AS332 Super Puma helicopter crashed into the Norwegian Sea while descending to land on an offshore platform. An engine overspeed light appeared during descent. Subsequent investigation found multiple fatigue cracks in the splined sleeve of the high-speed bendix shaft, which disintegrated and severed the shaft, causing catastrophic overspeed of the right-hand power turbine and burst, destroying both engines. The helicopter became uncontrollable and descended uncontrollably into the sea.
probable_cause: Multiple fatigue cracks in the splined sleeve between the high-speed bendix shaft and right-hand engine, causing shaft disintegration, engine overspeed, turbine burst, and loss of control. Contributing factors were inadequate inspection program and lack of HUMS monitoring; crew could not recognize severity of intermittent overspeed alarm.

title: 1997 Namibia mid-air collision

summary: A German Air Force Tupolev Tu-154M and a USAF Lockheed C-141B Starlifter collided at 35,000 feet over the Atlantic off Namibia. title: Garuda Indonesia 152
summary: Airbus A300 crashed into mountainous woodlands during approach to Medan after the crew became confused about the correct approach direction. Air traffic control issued conflicting instructions and called the aircraft by the wrong callsign, causing the crew to disregard a critical instruction about approach direction. The crew, unfamiliar with the analog flight instrumentation on the A300B4 FFCC, lost vertical awareness while concentrating on lateral changes and descended below the assigned 2000 foot altitude, striking treetops at 1550 feet.
probable_cause: Confusion regarding approach direction resulted in the crew initiating a left turn instead of a right turn during radar vectoring. This confusion, combined with the crew's focus on lateral changes and inadequate vertical monitoring, caused descent below assigned altitude. Contributing factors included poor ATC vectoring, inadequate conversion training for pilots switching between A300 models with different instrumentation, and failure of the GPWS system.

title: Alaska Airlines 261

summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 261, a McDonnell Douglas MD-83 flying from Puerto Vallarta toward Seattle with a stop in San Francisco, suffered a catastrophic loss of pitch control on 31 January 2000 after the horizontal stabilizer trim system's jackscrew assembly failed from worn acme nut threads, and crashed into the Pacific Ocean near Anacapa Island, California, while diverting to Los Angeles. The crew struggled for over two hours with a jammed stabilizer, and when they finally freed it using the primary trim system, it moved to an extreme nose-down position, forcing the aircraft into a nosedive from about 31,050 ft. The NTSB attributed the crash to inadequate maintenance that allowed excessive jackscrew wear, killing all 88 aboard.

The plane dropped from about 31,050 ft to between 23,000 ft and lower in around 80 seconds.

The plane dropped from about 31,050 ft to between 23,000 ft and lower in around 80 seconds as both pilots struggled together to regain control of the aircraft.

At this excessive descent rate the aircraft entered vortex ring state, lost control, rolled inverted and impacted the ground nose-first. All 19 Marines aboard were killed.

summary: Wuhan Airlines Flight 343, a Xian Y-7, crashed on 22 June 2000 while attempting to land at Wuhan Wangjiadun Airport during severe weather. The aircraft circled the airport for 30 minutes in thunderstorm conditions with 451 thunderclaps in 10 minutes. The crew debated diverting but the captain decided to continue the approach. title: Gulf Air 072
summary: Gulf Air Flight 072, an Airbus A320-212 flying from Cairo to Bahrain, crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf 2 km from the airport on 23 August 2000, minutes after a go-around from a failed approach to Runway 12. The captain suffered spatial disorientation, applying a large nose-down input that produced a 15-degree dive; as the aircraft descended, the crew disregarded the GPWS 'sink rate' and 'Whoop, whoop, pull up' warnings while debating flap configuration instead. summary: An Ilyushin Il-76TD cargo flight crashed on 14 July 2001 a few seconds after takeoff from Chkalovsky Airport near Moscow. The aircraft was loaded 14 tons above its maximum takeoff weight of 191.9 tons due to a weighing error, with the actual weight approximately 204 tons. During takeoff rotation, the aircraft immediately listed to the left, and at 23 meters altitude the pilots shifted the horizontal stabilizer nose-down at 5.4 degrees to -3.9 degrees, which is forbidden during takeoff. title: Space Shuttle Columbia disaster
summary: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry on February 1, 2003, when a piece of insulating foam broke off from the external tank during launch and struck the thermal protection system tiles on the orbiter's left wing. The impact created a hole in the heat shield that went undetected during the mission. When Columbia re-entered the atmosphere, hot gases penetrated the damaged area, destroying the internal wing structure and causing the orbiter to become unstable and break apart over Texas and Louisiana, killing all seven astronauts.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by damage to Columbia's thermal protection system tiles on the left wing caused by foam insulation that broke off from the external tank during launch. The damage went undetected during the mission. During re-entry, hot atmospheric gases penetrated through the damaged heat shield and destroyed the internal wing structure, causing the orbiter to become aerodynamically unstable and break apart.

factors.evidence: The orbiter became unstable and broke apart during re-entry over Texas and Louisiana, with debris dispersing over a wide area.

Engineers at NASA did not initially notice the debris strike and could not determine the level of damage sustained because no camera had a clear view of the debris impact.

The certification and risk management process did not adequately address the known hazard of foam shedding from the external tank or assess the potential consequences of impact to the thermal protection system.
Similar foam shedding had occurred during previous Space Shuttle launches, causing damage ranging from minor to near-catastrophic, but the hazard was not resolved before the Columbia mission.

title: 2015 Eglin Air Force Base helicopter crash
summary: A Sikorsky UH-60M Black Hawk helicopter crashed into Santa Rosa Sound on 10 March 2015 during a night training exercise. The helicopter flew into dense coastal fog that created a degraded visual environment approximately 173 seconds after takeoff. Both pilots exhibited spatial disorientation and the aircraft came to zero knots indicated airspeed and began flying backwards. The pilots made increasingly erratic flight control inputs and put the aircraft into a spin. The aircraft began to lose altitude and crashed into the hostel block of the B. J. Medical College campus 0.9 nmi from the runway.

events.text: The Boeing 787-8 lifted off from runway 23 at Ahmedabad at 13:38:39 IST after a 62-second takeoff roll, with light winds of 6 knots and visibility of 6 km.
Three seconds after liftoff the fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF, causing loss of thrust in both engines, according to the front flight recorder.
The aircraft reached a maximum pressure altitude of around 625 ft and a maximum airspeed of 180 knots before it began to lose altitude.
After 32 seconds of flight the aircraft crashed into the hostel block of B. J. Medical College 0.9 nmi from the runway, its tail striking the campus canteen roof before it broke apart.
The wreckage and subsequent fire severely damaged five buildings including the student and resident doctors' hostels, and only one of the 242 occupants survived.

notes: Preliminary AAIB report only; the reason the fuel control switches moved to CUTOFF had not been determined at time of writing.

title: Emirates SkyCargo 9788
summary: A Boeing 747-400 cargo aircraft with inoperative engine four thrust reverser experienced an uncommanded engine surge on landing at Hong Kong. After touchdown, autobrakes disconnected and the captain took manual control while activating thrust reversers on engines 1-3. Thirty seconds after touchdown, engine four spooled to 95% forward thrust, causing the aircraft to veer left. The aircraft struck a ground vehicle and plunged into the South China Sea, with the fuselage separating, killing two ground staff while all four crew survived.
probable_cause: Engine number four remained at high forward thrust despite selection to idle during the landing rollout, causing directional control loss and runway excursion into the sea.

title: UPS Airlines 2976

The engine, with most of its pylon still attached, separated and tumbled over the wing. The aircraft descended rapidly, struck multiple buildings and vehicles, and crashed into an industrial area. title: 2026 Bolivian Air Force Hercules C-130 crash

location.name: El Alto International Airport, Costanera Avenue

summary: A 49-year-old Lockheed C-130H Hercules carrying newly printed banknotes for the Central Bank of Bolivia landed at El Alto during heavy hailstorm. After landing, the aircraft veered off the runway, breached the airport perimeter fence, and collided with more than a dozen vehicles on Costanera Avenue, killing 24 people including 4 children. Technical report revealed the aircraft was at maximum capacity with pressure from delayed schedule, making safe landing at El Alto's 4,000 meter altitude physically impossible per aerodynamic laws.

title: Air Canada Express 8646
summary: On 22 March 2026, a Bombardier CRJ900 operating Air Canada Express Flight 8646 collided with an airport firefighting truck (Oshkosh Striker 1500, Truck 1) on runway 4 at LaGuardia Airport while landing. The aircraft was on short final approach when air traffic control cleared the truck to cross the runway to respond to an emergency with United Airlines Flight 2384. The controller immediately ordered the truck to stop but could not prevent the collision. The aircraft's cockpit and forward galley were destroyed, killing both pilots. A flight attendant seated on a jump-seat near the cockpit was ejected onto the runway and injured.

title: 2026 Colombian Air Force Lockheed C-130 crash
summary: A Colombian Air Force C-130H departed Caucayá Airport at 9:50 AM carrying 113 Army personnel, 2 police officers and 11 crew members on a troop transport mission. The aircraft was destroyed by post-crash fire and ammunition detonated. Fifty-seven occupants survived with injuries but 69 were killed. The investigation was ongoing, examining three hypotheses: mechanical failure, pilot error, or excess weight.

summary: A Cessna 208B Grand Caravan sightseeing aircraft crashed near Nazca, Peru on 1 August 2026 while performing a flight over the Nazca Lines. During cruise, the pilots declared a loss of control emergency. Strong winds, locally called Paracas winds, often exceeding 40 kilometers per hour, hit the region in days prior to the crash, bringing large quantities of sand and dust at high altitudes reducing visibility. The aircraft descended out of control and broke up in mid-air, killing all thirteen occupants.
